title: Thiamidol (isobutylamido thiazolyl resorcinol)
headline: A human-tyrosinase inhibitor with one sizable vehicle-controlled trial (melasma score down about 36% vs 16% on vehicle at 12 weeks). The trial was Fitzpatrick III-V, mostly Thai, brand-linked, and the benefit showed in melasma but not in post-inflammatory marks, freckles or lentigines.
evidenceTier: Randomized vehicle-controlled trial (200 people, 12 weeks) + uncontrolled real-world study + small pilots; brand-affiliated authors on most
fit: The mechanism (enzyme inhibition, not exfoliation) suits pigment-prone deep skin. But the one large trial was Fitzpatrick III-V, showed benefit only in melasma, and tested a 0.2% cream, while the retail products are alcohol-forward serums with an undisclosed percentage. Untested head to head against hydroquinone, azelaic acid or tranexamic acid.
displaces: Only an existing non-hydroquinone brightening serum used in the off-cycle slot. If that slot is already filled, it fits nowhere: adding it as a further pigment step is the usual failure.
estimateNote: Prices are as listed on retailer pages on 12 Oct 2026, not brand pages. Anything marked EST is a guess.

cost.label: Canada
cost.value: C$61.92 (Skin Perfecting Serum 30 ml, one retailer, one unit left); C$99.60 (Dual Serum 30 ml, another retailer, 'notify me' shown, so possibly unavailable). Retailer pages, 12 Oct 2026.

cost.label: UK
cost.value: £33.75 on offer, was £45.00 (Dual Serum 30 ml, Boots, in stock). 12 Oct 2026.

cost.label: EU
cost.value: sold as Eucerin Anti-Pigment serums; price not found

buzzCheck: Price does not track evidence here. The evidence is for the active in a 0.2% cream. The retail serums list the same active but no percentage, and cost about C$62 to C$100 in Canada and £34 to £45 in the UK for 30 ml. Because the concentration is undisclosed, you cannot compare dose per dollar.
summaryPoints: Mechanism: thiamidol inhibits human tyrosinase, the rate-limiting enzyme of melanin synthesis. It is not an exfoliant class (my inference on what that means for pigment-prone skin).

Best trial (full text read): 200 people, Fitzpatrick III-V, mostly Thai, 0.2% cream twice daily with SPF 30, 12 weeks. Melasma score (mMASI) fell 36.1% vs 16.1% on vehicle. Patient-rated change and instrument colour readings did not differ, and PIH, freckles and lentigines showed no significant difference.

The retail products are serums, not the trial cream. Concentration is not stated on any listing. Two retailer-listed formulations carry alcohol high on the list and fragrance; one also carries a vitamin C derivative.
Price spread is wide for the same active: about C$62 vs C$100 for 30 ml in Canada, and £33.75 on offer in the UK (retailer pages, 12 Oct 2026).
toneData: Trial: Fitzpatrick III-V, mostly Thai, no breakdown by type. Real-world study: phototypes I-V. Nothing reported at VI.
fitLine: Plausible by mechanism; the tested cream and the retail serums are not the same product, and benefit was shown in melasma only.
timeline: Physician-scored melasma change separated from vehicle by weeks 8-12 in the trial

fitAxes.why: The active is not an exfoliant or acid class (my inference). But the two retailer-listed serum formulations I read list alcohol denat. second (one) or third (other), and fragrance. That is a formulation issue rather than an active issue, and it matters for a barrier-first routine.

No data on use alongside retinoids. One listed formulation contains sodium ascorbyl phosphate (a vitamin C derivative), so check it against your vitamin C and retinoid sequencing rules before layering. Introduce alone first.

Ingredient lists read from retailer pages. One lists isopropyl palmitate and cetearyl isononanoate high up (fatty esters often flagged on comedogenicity lists; not verified for you). No breakout data in the trials.
UV and visible light drive pigment. A brand-run pilot suggests thiamidol blunts visible-light darkening in healthy skin. Not a substitute for tinted, iron-oxide sun protection.

dossier.whatItIs: Thiamidol (INCI: Isobutylamido Thiazolyl Resorcinol) is a synthetic resorcinol derivative developed by Beiersdorf and identified through screening against human tyrosinase rather than the mushroom enzyme older actives were tested on. It is the featured active in Eucerin's Anti-Pigment range. It is a cosmetic ingredient in the markets I looked at; I did not verify its regulatory status in every country.

structure.note: Flat 2D drawing generated from the structure string with RDKit. The formula (C13H14N2O3S), molecular weight (278.33) and chemical name N-[4-(2,4-dihydroxyphenyl)thiazol-2-yl]isobutyramide match supplier listings for CAS 1428450-95-6 seen in search results; I could not open PubChem. Stereochemistry is not relevant (no stereocentres).

steps: Thiamidol binds human tyrosinase and inhibits it (stated in the papers I read; the binding data are not in the abstracts I read).
Less tyrosinase activity means less conversion of tyrosine to melanin precursors.
Less melanin synthesis means less new pigment in spots or after UV or visible-light exposure.
mechanism.inferenceFlag: The abstracts I read report outcomes (colour, mMASI), not the enzyme chemistry. Mechanism statements come from the authors' framing and a review abstract. Whether the effect holds in epidermis with high melanocyte activity is inference.
mechanism.diagramCaption: Thiamidol -> human tyrosinase inhibited -> less melanin made -> less pigment (authors' model)

flow.label: Applied as 0.2% cream (RCT)
flow.note: The randomized trial used a 0.2% cream for 12 weeks versus vehicle.

flow.label: Inhibits human tyrosinase
flow.note: Stated in all four abstracts as the defining property of the molecule. Not independently verified here.

flow.label: Less melanin synthesis
flow.note: Follows from the enzyme's role. Not directly measured in the abstracts I read.

flow.label: Blunts UVB- and visible-light-induced darkening
flow.note: Two small studies in healthy volunteers (a UVB pilot and a visible-light study); the second is by the brand owner.

flow.label: mMASI fell 36% vs 16% on vehicle
flow.note: Physician-scored from standardized photographs in 196 completers. Patient-rated and digital-colour differences were not significant.

studies.cite: Lekhavat C, Rojanamatin J, Suphannaphong M, Kolbe L. Efficacy and Tolerability of 0.2% Thiamidol Cream for Facial Hyperpigmentation: A Randomized, Double-Blind, and Vehicle-Controlled Study. Dermatol Ther (Heidelb). 2026;16(3):1551-1565.
studies.readDepth: Full text (open access, PMC) read 12 Oct 2026
studies.design: Randomized, double-blind, vehicle-controlled, 12 weeks. 200 randomized, 196 completed. Registered NCT03926845.
studies.who: 200 adults (84% women), Fitzpatrick III-V, Southeast Asian, mostly Thai; the authors call the population relatively homogeneous. Diagnoses included melasma (the main analysis group), 66 with post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, 28 freckles, 12 solar lentigo; the paper does not explain how these overlap.
results: mMASI reduction from baseline, thiamidol vs vehicle: 11.8% vs 5.4% (week 4), 27.9% vs 13.6% (week 8), 36.1% vs 16.1% (week 12), all P<0.001.
Physician global assessment (melasma): slight to moderate improvement at weeks 8 and 12.
Patient global assessment and digital colour analysis: no significant difference between groups.
Freckles, solar lentigo and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation: no significant between-group difference on physician assessment (small subgroups, so inconclusive).
Used twice daily on the whole face with an SPF 30 UVA-protective sunscreen; other pigment treatments were prohibited.
studies.effectSize: Roughly 20 percentage points more mMASI reduction than vehicle at 12 weeks (arithmetic from the reported percentages).
studies.placebo: The vehicle group improved by 16% on mMASI, so a large share of the Thiamidol arm's change is not specific to the active.
studies.material: Not established. The physician-scored change moved, but patient-rated and instrument measures did not separate the groups.
studies.adverse: No significant adverse events. Brief itching without redness or swelling at week 4 (3 thiamidol, 2 vehicle) and week 8 (1 vs 2), resolving on its own. No hypopigmentation. 4 of 100 thiamidol participants withdrew (time constraints); none on vehicle.
studies.conflict: Funded by Beiersdorf Thailand, which supplied the cream; Beiersdorf AG paid the publication fee and holds the thiamidol patent. One author is a Beiersdorf employee involved in design and manuscript review, not in analysis. Other authors report no disclosures.
studies.limits: Single country, Fitzpatrick III-V only, no phototype breakdown. Melasma drives the result; other types were small subgroups. Tested a 0.2% cream, not the retail serums. No follow-up after stopping.

studies.cite: Schuster B, Rogers T, Vendruscolo C, et al. Real-world evidence for the efficacy and tolerability of an isobutylamido-thiazolyl-resorcinol (Thiamidol)-containing skincare regimen on facial hyperpigmentation and overall skin appearance: A multi-centre study in 11 European countries. Int J Cosmet Sci. 2026.
studies.design: Multi-centre, uncontrolled, open-label, 12 weeks, 11 European countries; regimen containing Thiamidol (not Thiamidol alone).
studies.who: 629 completers, 97.8% women, mean age 47, phototypes I-V. Phototype VI not included.
results: Reported relative improvements at 12 weeks: skin evenness 91%, radiance 82%, smoothness 73%; mMASI -76%.
Dermatologists rated tolerability very good in 81.1% of participants.
studies.effectSize: Large percentages from an uncontrolled study with a multi-product regimen. They cannot be attributed to Thiamidol alone.
studies.material: Not established; the percentages are relative and uncontrolled.
studies.adverse: Not detailed in the abstract beyond the tolerability ratings.
studies.limits: No control arm, regimen rather than single ingredient, brand-run, no phototype VI. Treat as a safety and tolerability signal, not an efficacy estimate.

studies.cite: Mann T, Eggers K, Rogers T, et al. Visible light induces skin darkening in vivo: comparative pilot studies reveal enhanced susceptibility in melasma and its mitigation by a human tyrosinase inhibitor. Photochem Photobiol Sci. 2026;25(2):299-306.
studies.design: Pilot in vivo studies: visible light and UV exposure on melasma and perilesional skin; Thiamidol versus vehicle on repeated visible-light irradiation in healthy skin.
studies.who: Melasma patients and healthy volunteers; sample sizes and phototypes are not in the abstract.
results: Melasma lesions darkened more than surrounding skin after visible light.
In healthy skin, Thiamidol significantly reduced visible-light-induced darkening compared with vehicle.
studies.placebo: Vehicle control in the healthy-skin part.
studies.material: Not established; an induced-darkening model, not treatment of existing spots.
studies.conflict: All authors are from Beiersdorf R&D.
studies.limits: Pilot, brand-run, abstract only. Visible light matters for deep skin tones, but this does not show the product replaces tinted, iron-oxide sun protection.

studies.cite: Vachiramon V, Kositkuljorn C, Leerunyakul K, Chanprapaph K. Isobutylamido thiazolyl resorcinol for prevention of UVB-induced hyperpigmentation. J Cosmet Dermatol. 2020;20(3):987-992.
studies.design: Randomized, single-blinded, split-arm pilot; 3 weeks of application then UVB-induced spots.
studies.who: 30 healthy participants, Bangkok, Thailand. Phototype not stated in the abstract.
results: After UVB induction, the Thiamidol-treated arm had a significantly lower lightness index than control and returned to normal colour earlier.
studies.limits: 30 healthy people, UVB-induced spots only, abstract only. Single-blinded.

claimsCheck.claim: Clinically proven to reduce dark spots (brand-style claim)
claimsCheck.status: Partly supported: one vehicle-controlled trial shows a melasma-score difference. It did not show a difference for post-inflammatory marks, freckles or lentigines, or on patient-rated and instrument measures.

claimsCheck.source: Not a claim I found sourced
claimsCheck.status: Not supported: the trial was Fitzpatrick III-V, the real-world study I-V, and nothing at VI was reported.

claimsCheck.claim: The retail serum delivers the trial result
claimsCheck.status: Not established: the trial used a 0.2% cream and no listing states the serum's concentration.

howToUse: Treat it as a swap into the brightening slot, not an addition. If a non-hydroquinone brightener is already in use, trial this in its place for the full 12 weeks the trial used.
The trial used 0.2% cream twice daily on the whole face with an SPF 30 UVA sunscreen and no other pigment treatments. A retail serum with an undisclosed percentage is not the same test.
Sun protection is part of any pigment routine: visible light is implicated in a brand pilot, so tinted, iron-oxide protection is the larger lever.

Introduce it alone for one to two weeks before pairing it with an acid or retinoid, because combination data are absent. If using the formulation with a vitamin C derivative, check your sequencing rules first.

expect.what: Little visible change. In the RCT the mMASI difference was modest at week 4.
The range in which the trial separated from vehicle. Expect gradual change, and note the vehicle group also improved.
No follow-up data in the abstracts I read.

dossier.contraindications: No significant adverse events in the trial; brief itching in a few people on both arms. Not tested in pregnancy or alongside prescription depigmenting agents; treat that as unknown. Formulation note: high alcohol content and fragrance in the listed serums are a barrier consideration.
dossier.sideBenefits: None shown. The visible-light result is a protective effect on induced darkening in healthy skin, not a treatment effect.
wouldChangeVerdict: Independent (non-brand) replication, ideally in Fitzpatrick V-VI
Trial results for post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation specifically
A head-to-head or add-on trial against hydroquinone, tranexamic acid or azelaic acid
A stated thiamidol percentage in a product that is easy to buy
A formulation without high alcohol content and fragrance, if your routine is barrier-first
dossier.transfer: Does it transfer to deeper skin? The mechanism (blocking the enzyme that makes melanin) is not tone-specific, so some effect is plausible. But the trial was Fitzpatrick III-V and did not break results down by type, the real-world study stops at phototype V, benefit was shown in melasma and not in post-inflammatory marks, and the trial product was a cream, not the retail serums. That is inference, not evidence.
confidence: Full text read for the 2026 randomized trial (PMC). Abstract only for the other three studies.
Product ingredient lists and prices read from retailer pages on 12 Oct 2026, not brand pages; formulations may differ by market and over time.
Not verified: the thiamidol percentage in any retail product, EU, Korean and Japanese prices, and the funding of the 2020 pilot.
Source types: one randomized trial, one uncontrolled real-world study, two small pilots; all with brand-linked authors except possibly the 2020 pilot (not checked).
